Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Recently, specially designed functional surfaces such as superhydrophobic surfaces, inspired by the “lotus effect” in nature, have attracted extensive attention because of their widespread application in materials science and engineering technology. (1−12) A superhydrophobic surface exhibits extremely high water resistance: the static contact angle of water is larger than 150° and the dynamic sliding angle is smaller than 10°. (13−15) Superhydrophobic surfaces are generally created by a micro–nanostructured rough surface and low-surface-energy material modification. (9,16−25) As water repellency is important in practical applications including self-cleaning, (26−28) oil–water separation, (29−37) corrosion protection, (38) and anti-icing, (39) there are a number of research works on superhydrophobic surfaces. For example, Ge et al. (40) reported that a transparent and superamphiphobic surface could be created from strings of amphiphilic silica nanoparticles dispersed in an amphiphilic sol solution by a one-step spray-coating method. Li et al. (41) fabricated a translucent and superhydrophobic polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) coating on a glass substrate by introducing roughness using SiO2 nanoparticles with an aerosol-assisted chemical vapor deposition method. Wu et al. (42) synthesized emulsions by a one-step method using nanoparticles, PTES, waterborne epoxy resin, and ethanol and prepared an environmentally friendly and stable superhydrophobic film by simply spraying them on the surface of a substrate. Although research on superhydrophobic surfaces has made significant progress, most preparation methods are still complicated, requiring special conditions and/or expensive equipment, which limit their practical application. For superhydrophobic surfaces, high transparency is a requirement in many practical applications. (4,43−52) As we know, the transparency of coatings generally becomes worse when the surface roughness increases because light scattering occurs when light strikes the rough surface, causing the surface to exhibit translucence or opaqueness. Therefore, light scattering can be attenuated by reducing the roughness of the surface, making the surface transparent. (53) Previous studies on transparent and durable superhydrophobic surfaces were mainly related to carbon derivatives, polymers, and silicon nanoparticles. (54) Gao et al. (55) reported that a superhydrophobic surface could be obtained using PDMS as the binder, tetrahydrofuran as the solvent, and water as the nonsolvent by phase separation. Results showed that transmittance decreased by less than 10%. Alawajji et al. (56) successfully fabricated transparent superhydrophobic polytetrafluoroethylene thin films using pulsed laser deposition with various deposition times at room temperature, and the transmission rate could be as high as 90%. Unfortunately, although the desired hydrophobicity and transparency were obtained, the robustness and wear resistance of the film were not good because of the flexibility of the polymer. In this paper, we present a simple, fast, and environmentally friendly one-step spray coating method for preparing superhydrophobic coatings on different substrates using readily available materials such as PDMS and SiO2 nanoparticles. When hydrophilic SiO2 and hydrophobic SiO2 nanoparticles are mixed in a certain ratio and blended with PDMS, a roughly hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface can be obtained, wherein PDMS is used as both a low surface energy modifier and an adhesive. After being exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light for 72 h, peeled off for 250 cycles by a tape, and immersed in a strong acid/base solution for 72 h, the superhydrophobic coatings still show good water resistance, revealing good durability. In addition, the coatings can maintain sufficient transparency, allowing them to be used in a wide range of applications. Based on their excellent superhydrophobicity and lipophilicity, the coatings can be used for large-scale applications in self-cleaning and oil–water separation. 2. Tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) and hexane were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Ditin butyl dilaurate (C32H64O4Sn) and hydrophilic fumed nanosilica (7–40 nm) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. Hydrophobic gas-phase nanosilica (7–40 nm) was purchased from Aladdin Biotechnology Corporation. 2.2. fetched_contents.text: Superhydrophobic anti-corrosion coatings for metal surfaces: a systematic review from fabrication to performance Abstract Metals are fundamental to numerous industrial and everyday applications, yet corrosion poses significant economic and safety challenges. Superhydrophobic coatings have shown great promise in mitigating these issues by effectively minimizing the retention and penetration of corrosive electrolytes. Through multiple protective mechanisms – such as water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion – these coatings isolate the metal substrate from direct contact with corrosive media, thereby significantly improving corrosion resistance. As a result, superhydrophobic coatings have attracted considerable research interest in the field of metal anti-corrosion. This review summarizes recent advances in superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection, systematically elaborating on their protective mechanisms and fabrication techniques. Fabrication techniques and surface engineering methods

Major coating fabrication methods and their advantages/disadvantages

The evidence points to a broad family of superhydrophobic coating fabrication strategies, with a clear distinction between top-down and bottom-up approaches. One review explicitly notes that fabrication methods include top-down methods such as laser ablation and etching, as well as bottom-up methods like sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R3]. A second source adds that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by creating the required surface roughness on a low-surface-energy material [N2-R4]. This suggests that the most common methods are either structuring the surface directly (top-down) or building up the coating layer by layer from molecular or particulate components (bottom-up).

The advantages of these methods vary by approach. Etching and template-based methods are attractive because they can produce well-controlled surface roughness and nanostructures, as shown in the one-step etching fabrication of a CuO/Cu2O/CuCl composite surface [N2-R2]. Similarly, sol–gel and templating can offer fine control over morphology [N2-R3]. However, these methods can also be more complex or require specialized equipment. The same source notes that fabrication techniques often still suffer from complexity, special conditions, or expensive equipment, which limits practical application [N2-F2]. For example, the one-step spray-coating method described in the PDMS/silica nanocomposite study is presented as a simpler, environmentally friendly alternative, but it still requires careful control of composition and spraying parameters to avoid excessive thickness or reduced transparency [N1-F1].

Surface roughness and texture engineering strategies

A central strategy for superhydrophobicity is surface roughness combined with low-surface-energy materials. The PDMS/silica study explicitly states that superhydrophobic surfaces are generally created by a micro–nanostructured rough surface and low-surface-energy material modification [N1-F1]. The same source describes a one-step spray-coating method that blends hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles with PDMS to form a hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader review, which emphasizes surface roughness as a key factor in superhydrophobic design [N2-R4].

The evidence also highlights texture engineering through the choice of particles and morphology. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study shows that mixing hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles in a certain ratio can produce a hierarchical structure that improves superhydrophobicity [N1-F1]. A separate review notes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by roughness engineering, with the roughness of the surface affecting transparency because light scattering increases with roughness [N1-F1]. This indicates that texture engineering is not only about creating roughness, but also about balancing roughness with optical and mechanical performance.

Chemical modification and functionalization approaches

Chemical modification is a recurring theme. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS as both a low-surface-energy modifier and an adhesive, and it also incorporates silica nanoparticles through a sol-gel-like route [N1-F1]. The same source notes that PDMS can be combined with SiO2 nanoparticles to form a rough structure, which is essential for superhydrophobicity [N1-R1]. Another search result explicitly states that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity or superoleophobicity [N1-R4], which reinforces that functionalization often involves adding low-surface-energy polymers or fluorinated components.

The evidence also supports the use of other functional components. The one-step etching fabrication example uses chemical etching and modification to create a superhydrophobic surface [N2-R2]. The broader fabrication review mentions vapor deposition, etching modification, sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R5], showing that chemical modification can be part of the fabrication process itself. In the steel-specific anti-corrosion context, a stearic acid–yttrium (SA–Y) superhydrophobic coating is prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2], which illustrates how chemical modification can be integrated into coating formation.

Steel-specific surface preparation and how it affects coating performance

Steel surface preparation matters because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The steel-specific anti-corrosion review notes that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This implies that surface preparation must support good adhesion and prevent corrosion pathways.

The evidence also shows that surface preparation can involve cleaning and conditioning. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study describes substrate cleaning with deionized water and alcohol before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared on low manganese steel by electrodeposition, which indicates that steel chemistry and surface state can influence coating formation [N4-R2]. The corrosion protection review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4], which means that even minor surface contamination or poor conditioning can degrade performance.

Overall, steel-specific preparation is important because it affects adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. The evidence suggests that successful coating performance depends on a combination of proper surface cleaning, conditioning, and chemical modification, rather than coating formulation alone [N4-R2][N1-F1][N6-F3].

Mechanisms and performance enhancement strategies

How the coating suppresses biofouling and prevents microbial adhesion

The evidence points to several mechanisms by which coatings suppress biofouling. One mechanism is surface chemistry repulsion, including hydration layer formation, surface charge repulsion, hydrophobic foul-release, and other biofouling-inhibiting effects [N3-R4]. Another search result describes zwitterionic hydrogel nanolayers that resist biofouling through the foulant repulsion of hydration shells and bactericidal effects [N3-R2]. A related study on photografted zwitterionic materials notes that antifouling effects are achievable across a broad range of cross-link densities, while maintaining mechanical functionality [N3-R1]. This indicates that biofouling suppression is not limited to one pathway but can combine multiple mechanisms.

The anti-biofouling strategy can also involve integrated antifouling and antimicrobial approaches. One source states that integrated antifouling and antimicrobial approaches are developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N3-R5]. This suggests that coatings may be designed to both repel microorganisms and kill them, especially in high-shear environments where fouling-release becomes important [N3-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a layered strategy: repelling microbes through surface chemistry, preventing adhesion through hydration or charge effects, and optionally killing organisms through antimicrobial components.

Strategies to improve durability and resistance to environmental stress

Durability is addressed through both material selection and fabrication methods. The PDMS/silica study shows that a one-step spray-coating method can produce coatings that remain superhydrophobic even after 250 tape peel cycles, UV exposure, and immersion in strong acid/base solutions for 72 h [N1-F1]. This is a clear durability demonstration. Another review emphasizes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be durable if transparency and roughness are balanced to reduce light scattering [N1-F1], which suggests that environmental stress is not only mechanical but also optical and chemical.

A separate review on recent advances in superhydrophobic materials development highlights durable nanostructures and intrinsic durability as key considerations [N5-R2]. This implies that durability is achieved through material architecture rather than surface chemistry alone. The same review also notes that the integration of durable nanostructures improves performance [N5-R1], which aligns with the broader idea that mechanical robustness is essential for long-term use.

Hybrid or multifunctional design features and their benefits

Hybrid or multifunctional designs are a major theme. The evidence repeatedly refers to multifunctional systems. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS and silica nanoparticles together to create a superhydrophobic coating with good self-cleaning ability [N1-F1]. The dual-coating method combines polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine and fluorinated silica to create superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces [N1-R2]. This indicates that multifunctionality is often achieved by combining different materials or functional groups.

Another example is the use of zwitterionic materials with photografting to maintain antifouling while preserving mechanical properties [N3-R1]. This is a hybrid design because it combines antifouling chemistry with mechanical functionality. The review on recent advances also emphasizes bio-inspired design and durable nanostructures, showing that multifunctionality is not only about anti-biofouling but also about long-term performance [N5-R2][N5-R1].

Self-healing or stimuli-responsive features and their role in long-term stability

Self-healing and stimuli-responsive features are important for long-term stability. The review on recent advances in self-healing chemistries and approaches covers intrinsic and extrinsic self-healing strategies [N5-R3]. A separate study on superhydrophobic coatings with photothermal self-healing shows excellent self-healing performance in response to chemical and microstructure damage, with rapid self-healing under 1 sun [N5-R4]. This demonstrates that stimuli-responsive systems can repair damage and maintain performance.

The evidence also supports broader stimuli-responsive strategies. A review on smart antibacterial antifouling strategies notes that a variety of smart strategies have been developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N5-R5]. While this excerpt is not specific to superhydrophobic coatings, it reinforces the general trend toward responsive materials. Together, these sources show that self-healing and stimuli-responsive features extend stability by repairing damage and adapting to environmental changes [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Overall, the coating suppresses biofouling through surface chemistry repulsion, hydration, charge effects, and optionally antimicrobial action [N3-R4][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Durability is improved by combining low-surface-energy materials with robust fabrication methods and by balancing roughness with transparency [N1-F1][N5-R2]. Hybrid or multifunctional designs combine anti-biofouling with mechanical or chemical functionality [N1-R2][N3-R1]. Self-healing and stimuli-responsive features improve long-term stability by repairing damage and adapting to environmental stress [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Materials and composition of superhydrophobic anti-biofouling coatings

Main polymer or matrix materials used in the coating

The evidence clearly identifies silicone-based and fluorinated materials as the main polymeric materials for superhydrophobicity. The PDMS/silica study explicitly states that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity or superoleophobicity [N1-R4]. A separate review describes polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) as a central material, noting that PDMS can be combined with SiO2 nanoparticles to form a rough structure that results in superhydrophobicity [N1-R1]. The dual-coating method further combines polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine and fluorinated silica to create superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces [N1-R2]. This indicates that the main matrix materials are PDMS and fluorinated or silicone-based polymers.

Low-surface-energy additives and functional groups that contribute to superhydrophobicity

Low-surface-energy additives are central to superhydrophobicity. The PDMS/silica study explains that superhydrophobic surfaces are created by a micro–nanostructured rough surface and low-surface-energy material modification [N1-F1]. It also states that PDMS is used as both a low-surface-energy modifier and an adhesive [N1-F1]. The same source shows that hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles are blended with PDMS to form a hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface [N1-F1]. The review on superhydrophobic materials notes that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity [N1-R4], which supports the role of fluorinated or silicone-based functional groups.

The evidence also points to the importance of particle chemistry. The one-step spray-coating method uses hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles in a certain ratio to create a hierarchical structure [N1-F1]. The review on superhydrophobic surfaces emphasizes that low-surface-energy modification is a core part of the design [N2-R4]. Together, these sources show that superhydrophobicity is achieved through a combination of low-surface-energy polymer matrices and carefully selected additives that control roughness and chemistry.

Anti-biofouling agents and how they are incorporated into the material

Anti-biofouling incorporation is often achieved through functionalization or hybrid components. The PDMS/silica study describes a dual-coating method that includes fluorinated silica and polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine to create superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces [N1-R2]. This implies that anti-biofouling can be incorporated by adding fluorinated or bacteriostatic components. The zwitterionic hydrogel nanolayer study states that enhanced biofouling resistance is derived from the foulant repulsion of hydration shells and bactericidal effects [N3-R2], indicating that biofouling suppression can be built into the material chemistry.

The evidence also supports photografting as a way to incorporate antifouling functionality. The photografted zwitterionic materials study notes that antifouling effects can be achieved across a broad range of cross-linker concentrations, while maintaining mechanical functionality [N3-R1]. This shows that anti-biofouling agents are not limited to surface additives; they can be chemically integrated into the coating structure itself. The review on biomass-based antifouling coatings further states that materials inhibit biofouling through mechanisms such as hydration layer formation, surface charge repulsion, hydrophobic foul-release, and others [N3-R4], reinforcing that anti-biofouling is a functional design goal rather than a separate layer.

Materials designed to also suppress corrosion and how they differ from pure anti-biofouling systems

Corrosion-suppressing coatings differ from pure anti-biofouling systems by incorporating additional protective mechanisms. The anti-corrosion review explains that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This means that corrosion protection is not just about surface wetting but also about blocking corrosive electrolyte penetration and improving adhesion.

The evidence also shows that corrosion protection can be achieved through hybrid multifunctionality. The SA–Y superhydrophobic coating is prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel, indicating that corrosion protection is part of the coating strategy [N4-R2]. The review on self-healing superhydrophobic coatings notes that superhydrophobic surfaces can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4]. In addition, the Ni-Al layered double hydroxide study presents a highly stable, eco-friendly superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel via a facile two-step process [N6-R5].

These materials differ from pure anti-biofouling systems because they must address both biofouling and corrosion simultaneously. While pure anti-biofouling coatings may focus on surface chemistry and repulsion, anti-corrosion coatings must also prevent electrolyte ingress, inhibit electrochemical reactions, and enhance interfacial adhesion [N6-F3][N6-R4]. The corrosion-specific review explicitly frames these coatings as systems that combine water repellency with electrochemical inhibition [N6-R1]. Therefore, the main distinction is that anti-corrosion coatings are multifunctional, whereas pure anti-biofouling systems may prioritize only biofouling prevention.

Steel-specific surface preparation and compatibility

Steel surface preparation steps and why they matter

Steel surface preparation is critical because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The evidence shows that preparation often begins with cleaning. The PDMS/silica study describes substrate cleaning with deionized water and alcohol before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared on low manganese steel by electrodeposition, which implies that surface state and metal chemistry are important for coating formation [N4-R2]. The anti-corrosion review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media, suggesting that a clean, well-prepared surface is needed to prevent contamination from the outset [N6-F3].

Why surface preparation matters includes adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. A clean surface improves coating adhesion and reduces defects such as delamination or poor bonding [N1-F1][N4-R2]. It also affects how the coating interacts with the steel substrate: if the surface is contaminated or not properly conditioned, the coating may not spread evenly or may fail at the interface [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The evidence further indicates that preparation affects long-term performance, because poor surface conditioning can compromise the protective role of the coating [N6-F3].

How coating adhesion and performance are affected by steel chemistry

Steel chemistry is important because different steel compositions can influence adhesion and performance. The SA–Y coating is prepared on low manganese steel, which shows that the specific steel chemistry can determine the fabrication route [N4-R2]. The anti-corrosion review notes that superhydrophobic coatings improve interfacial adhesion, which is especially important on metals where adhesion can be weak without surface treatment [N6-F3]. Another review explicitly states that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection are designed to isolate the metal from corrosive media through enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-R1].

The evidence also suggests that steel-specific chemistry can affect coating durability and corrosion resistance. The Ni-Al layered double hydroxide coating is described as a highly stable, eco-friendly superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel [N6-R5]. This implies that the choice of steel and any alloying elements may influence how well the coating performs. Because the evidence does not provide a detailed comparative table of steel chemistries, the exact effects are limited to the examples cited, but the general principle is clear: steel chemistry affects adhesion, corrosion resistance, and coating compatibility [N4-R2][N6-F3][N6-R5].

Corrosion protection and long-term stability considerations

Corrosion protection is a major consideration because superhydrophobic coatings are often designed to reduce electrolyte retention and inhibit electrochemical reactions. The anti-corrosion review explains that these coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. It also states that superhydrophobic coatings can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4]. This indicates that long-term stability depends on both the coating’s ability to stay intact and its ability to block corrosion pathways.

The review also notes that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection have been summarized in terms of fabrication techniques and performance [N6-R2]. The evidence suggests that long-term stability is not only about the coating’s initial performance but also about how it degrades over time. The SA–Y coating example and the Ni-Al layered double hydroxide study both show that steel-specific anti-corrosion coatings can be fabricated with durability in mind [N4-R2][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide detailed failure modes or degradation timelines, so the claim is supported only by the stated protective mechanisms rather than empirical failure data.

Examples of steel-specific anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling coupling strategies

The evidence provides several examples of coupling strategies. One example is the SA–Y superhydrophobic coating prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2]. This is a direct coupling strategy because the coating is designed for corrosion protection on steel. Another example is the Ni-Al layered double hydroxide superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel via a facile two-step process [N6-R5]. This shows that corrosion protection can be combined with superhydrophobicity.

The anti-corrosion review also states that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection are designed to isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, electrochemical inhibition, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This is a general coupling strategy that combines anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling principles, because both require surface protection from environmental attack. The evidence also supports the broader idea that multifunctional coatings can combine anti-biofouling with corrosion resistance, as seen in the PDMS/silica study’s emphasis on self-cleaning and anti-icing properties alongside superhydrophobicity [N1-F1].

In summary, steel surface preparation matters because it affects adhesion, compatibility, and performance [N1-F1][N4-R2][N6-F3]. Steel chemistry influences how well the coating adheres and how long it remains effective [N4-R2][N6-R5]. Corrosion protection depends on water repellency, electrochemical inhibition, and interfacial adhesion [N6-F3][N6-R4]. Steel-specific coupling strategies include electrodeposition on low manganese steel, Ni-Al layered double hydroxide coatings, and multifunctional anti-corrosion/anti-biofouling designs [N4-R2][N6-R5][N6-F3].

## Key materials and techniques used to develop and enhance superhydrophobic anti-biofouling polymer coatings on steel surfaces

Superhydrophobic anti-biofouling polymer coatings on steel surfaces are developed using a combination of materials science and surface engineering principles. The core idea is to combine **low-surface-energy polymer matrices**, **surface roughness engineering**, and **anti-biofouling chemistry** into a single coating system, while ensuring the coating is compatible with steel and durable under environmental stress. Below is an integrated synthesis of the key materials, fabrication techniques, mechanisms, and steel-specific considerations.

---

## 1) Main materials and composition

### A) Polymer or matrix materials
The evidence identifies **silicone-based and fluorinated materials** as the main polymeric platforms for superhydrophobicity [N1-R4]. **Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)** is a central matrix material in many studies, often combined with silica nanoparticles to create roughness and superhydrophobicity [N1-R1]. Fluorinated silanes and fluorinated silica are also important, because they contribute both low surface energy and chemical durability [N1-R2][N1-R4].

### B) Low-surface-energy additives and functional groups
Superhydrophobicity relies on a **low-surface-energy material** combined with **surface roughness** [N1-F1][N2-R4]. In the PDMS/silica study, PDMS acts as both a **low-surface-energy modifier** and an adhesive, while silica nanoparticles provide the **micro–nanostructured roughness** needed for water repellency [N1-F1]. The review on superhydrophobic materials emphasizes that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity [N1-R4]. This means that the functional groups contributing to superhydrophobicity are primarily silicone and fluorinated groups.

### C) Anti-biofouling agents and their incorporation
Anti-biofouling is achieved through functionalization or hybrid components. The dual-coating method combines **polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine** and **fluorinated silica** to create **superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces** [N1-R2]. Another strategy uses **zwitterionic hydrogel nanolayers**, which resist biofouling through **hydration shell repulsion** and **bactericidal effects** [N3-R2]. Photografted zwitterionic materials also show broad antifouling effects across different cross-linker concentrations while maintaining mechanical functionality [N3-R1]. These examples show that anti-biofouling agents are often incorporated by chemical functionalization rather than added as a separate layer.

### D) Corrosion-suppressing materials and their distinction from pure anti-biofouling systems
Corrosion-suppressing coatings differ from pure anti-biofouling systems because they must also protect the metal from corrosive attack. The anti-corrosion review explains that superhydrophobic coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media through **water repellency**, **inhibition of electrochemical reactions**, and **enhanced interfacial adhesion** [N6-F3]. This means corrosion protection is not just about repelling water, but also about blocking electrolyte ingress and improving adhesion. Examples include **SA–Y superhydrophobic coatings** prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2], and a **Ni-Al layered double hydroxide** superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel [N6-R5]. These systems combine anti-biofouling and anti-corrosion functionality, whereas pure anti-biofouling systems may prioritize only biofouling suppression.

---

## 2) Fabrication and surface engineering methods

### A) Major coating fabrication methods and their advantages/disadvantages
The evidence points to a broad family of fabrication methods, including **top-down** and **bottom-up** approaches. Top-down methods include **laser ablation**, **etching**, and **templating**, while bottom-up methods include **sol–gel**, **template-assisted**, **electrostatic spinning**, and **electrostatic methods** [N2-R3]. A separate review notes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by creating the required surface roughness on a low-surface-energy material [N2-R4].

The advantages of these methods vary. Etching and templating can produce well-controlled roughness and nanostructures [N2-R2], while sol–gel and templating offer fine morphological control [N2-R3]. However, many methods still suffer from **complexity**, **special conditions**, or **expensive equipment**, which limits practical application [N2-F2]. In contrast, the one-step spray-coating method for PDMS/silica is presented as a simpler, environmentally friendly alternative [N1-F1].

### B) Surface roughness and texture engineering strategies
A central strategy for superhydrophobicity is **surface roughness plus low-surface-energy material modification** [N1-F1]. The PDMS/silica study shows that mixing **hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles** in a certain ratio can produce a **hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface** [N1-F1]. The same study also explains that roughness affects transparency because light scattering increases with roughness [N1-F1]. This means texture engineering must balance **roughness**, **transparency**, and **mechanical robustness**.

### C) Chemical modification and functionalization approaches
Chemical modification is a recurring theme. PDMS is used as both a low-surface-energy modifier and an adhesive [N1-F1]. Silica nanoparticles are incorporated through a sol-gel-like route or by blending into the PDMS matrix [N1-F1][N1-R1]. Fluorinated silanes and fluorinated silica are also important because they contribute both low surface energy and chemical durability [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The broader fabrication review notes that **vapor deposition**, **etching modification**, **sol–gel**, **template**, **electrostatic spinning**, and **electrostatic methods** are all used in superhydrophobic fabrication [N2-R5].

### D) Steel-specific surface preparation and how it affects coating performance
Steel surface preparation is critical because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The PDMS/silica study describes cleaning with **deionized water and alcohol** before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared by electrodeposition on **low manganese steel**, showing that steel chemistry can determine the fabrication route [N4-R2]. The anti-corrosion review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media through **water repellency**, **inhibition of electrochemical reactions**, and **enhanced interfacial adhesion** [N6-F3]. This means that surface preparation affects not only adhesion but also long-term corrosion resistance.

The evidence also shows that steel chemistry affects coating performance. The SA–Y coating and the Ni-Al layered double hydroxide coating both demonstrate steel-specific anti-corrosion strategies [N4-R2][N6-R5]. This implies that the exact effects of steel chemistry depend on the alloy and processing route, but the general principle is clear: **clean, well-conditioned steel improves adhesion and durability** [N1-F1][N4-R2].

## 3) Mechanisms and performance enhancement strategies

### A) How the coating suppresses biofouling and prevents microbial adhesion
The evidence points to several biofouling suppression mechanisms. One is **hydration layer formation**, **surface charge repulsion**, **hydrophobic foul-release**, and other biofouling-inhibiting effects [N3-R4]. Zwitterionic hydrogel nanolayers resist biofouling through **hydration shell repulsion** and **bactericidal effects** [N3-R2]. Photografted zwitterionic materials also show broad antifouling effects while maintaining mechanical functionality [N3-R1]. Integrated antifouling and antimicrobial approaches are also developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N3-R5].

This means that anti-biofouling is not a single mechanism but often a combination of **repulsion**, **hydration**, **charge effects**, and optionally **antimicrobial action**. The evidence supports a layered strategy: repel microbes through surface chemistry, prevent adhesion through hydration or charge repulsion, and optionally kill organisms through antimicrobial components [N3-R4][N3-R2][N3-R5].

### B) Strategies to improve durability and resistance to environmental stress
Durability is improved through material selection, fabrication methods, and design choices. The PDMS/silica study shows that a one-step spray-coating method can produce coatings that remain superhydrophobic after **250 tape peel cycles**, **UV exposure**, and **72 h immersion in strong acid/base solutions** [N1-F1]. This is a clear demonstration of durability. The review on recent advances also emphasizes **durable nanostructures** and intrinsic durability [N5-R2]. This implies that durability is achieved through material architecture rather than surface chemistry alone.

Environmental resistance is also addressed by balancing roughness with transparency [N1-F1]. Light scattering from roughness can reduce transparency, so durable superhydrophobic coatings must minimize unnecessary roughness while preserving water repellency [N1-F1]. This shows that environmental stress is not only mechanical but also optical and chemical.

### C) Hybrid or multifunctional design features and their benefits
Hybrid or multifunctional designs are a major theme. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS and silica nanoparticles together to create a superhydrophobic coating with good self-cleaning ability [N1-F1]. The dual-coating method combines **polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine** and **fluorinated silica** to create **superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces** [N1-R2]. This indicates that multifunctionality is often achieved by combining different materials or functional groups.

Another example is the use of **zwitterionic materials** with **photografting** to maintain antifouling while preserving mechanical properties [N3-R1]. The review on recent advances also emphasizes **bio-inspired design** and **durable nanostructures**, showing that multifunctionality is not only about anti-biofouling but also about long-term performance [N5-R2][N5-R1].

### D) Self-healing or stimuli-responsive features and their role in long-term stability
Self-healing and stimuli-responsive features are important for long-term stability. A review on recent advances in self-healing chemistries and approaches covers both intrinsic and extrinsic self-healing strategies [N5-R3]. A separate study on superhydrophobic coatings with **photothermal self-healing** shows excellent self-healing performance in response to chemical and microstructure damage, with rapid self-healing under **1 sun** [N5-R4]. This demonstrates that stimuli-responsive systems can repair damage and maintain performance.

The evidence also supports broader smart strategies. A review on smart antibacterial antifouling strategies notes that a variety of smart strategies have been developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N5-R5]. While this excerpt is not specific to superhydrophobic coatings, it reinforces the general trend toward responsive materials. Together, these sources show that self-healing and stimuli-responsive features improve long-term stability by repairing damage and adapting to environmental changes [N5-R3][N5-R4].

## 4) Steel-specific surface preparation and compatibility

### A) Steel surface preparation steps and why they matter
Steel surface preparation is critical because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The evidence shows that preparation often begins with **cleaning**. The PDMS/silica study describes cleaning with **deionized water and alcohol** before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared by electrodeposition on **low manganese steel**, indicating that surface state and metal chemistry matter [N4-R2]. The anti-corrosion review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media, so preparation must begin with a clean surface [N6-F3].

### B) How coating adhesion and performance are affected by steel chemistry
Steel chemistry affects adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. The SA–Y coating example shows that the specific steel chemistry can determine the fabrication route [N4-R2]. The anti-corrosion review notes that superhydrophobic coatings improve **interfacial adhesion**, which is especially important on metals where adhesion can be weak without surface treatment [N6-F3]. Another review explicitly states that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection are designed to isolate the metal from corrosive media through **enhanced interfacial adhesion** [N6-R1].

The evidence also suggests that steel-specific chemistry can affect coating durability and corrosion resistance. The Ni-Al layered double hydroxide coating is described as a highly stable, eco-friendly superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel [N6-R5]. This implies that the choice of steel and any alloying elements may influence how well the coating performs. Because the evidence does not provide a detailed comparative table of steel chemistries, the exact effects are limited to the examples cited, but the general principle is clear: **steel chemistry affects adhesion, corrosion resistance, and coating compatibility** [N4-R2][N6-F3][N6-R5].

### C) Corrosion protection and long-term stability considerations
Corrosion protection is a major consideration because superhydrophobic coatings are often designed to reduce electrolyte retention and inhibit electrochemical reactions. The anti-corrosion review explains that these coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media through **water repellency**, **inhibition of electrochemical reactions**, and **enhanced interfacial adhesion** [N6-F3]. It also states that superhydrophobic coatings can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4]. This means long-term stability depends on both the coating’s ability to stay intact and its ability to block corrosion pathways.

The review also notes that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection have been summarized in terms of fabrication techniques and performance [N6-R2]. The evidence suggests that long-term stability is not only about the coating’s initial performance but also about how it degrades over time. The SA–Y coating example and the Ni-Al layered double hydroxide study both show that steel-specific anti-corrosion coatings can be fabricated with durability in mind [N4-R2][N6-R5]. However, the evidence does not provide detailed failure modes or degradation timelines, so the claim is supported only by the stated protective mechanisms rather than empirical failure data.

### D) Examples of steel-specific anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling coupling strategies
The evidence provides several examples of coupling strategies. One is the **SA–Y superhydrophobic coating** prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2]. This is a direct coupling strategy because the coating is designed for corrosion protection on steel. Another example is the **Ni-Al layered double hydroxide** superhydrophobic coating fabricated on steel via a facile two-step process [N6-R5]. This shows that corrosion protection can be combined with superhydrophobicity.

The anti-corrosion review also states that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection are designed to isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, electrochemical inhibition, and interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This is a general coupling strategy that combines anti-corrosion and anti-biofouling principles, because both require surface protection from environmental attack. The evidence also supports the broader idea that multifunctional coatings can combine anti-biofouling with corrosion resistance, as seen in the PDMS/silica study’s emphasis on self-cleaning and anti-icing properties alongside superhydrophobicity [N1-F1].

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

The key materials and techniques used to develop and enhance superhydrophobic anti-biofouling polymer coatings on steel surfaces are:

- **Main polymers/matrix materials**: **PDMS**, **fluorinated silanes**, and **fluorinated silica** [N1-R1][N1-R4][N1-R2].
- **Low-surface-energy additives**: silica nanoparticles, PDMS, and fluorinated components [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **Anti-biofouling agents**: zwitterionic materials, photografted zwitterionic structures, and integrated antimicrobial components [N3-R2][N3-R1][N3-R5].
- **Corrosion-suppressing materials**: SA–Y coatings, Ni-Al layered double hydroxide, and other anti-corrosion superhydrophobic systems [N4-R2][N6-R5].
- **Fabrication methods**: etching, templating, sol–gel, spray coating, electrodeposition, and vapor deposition [N2-R3][N2-R5][N1-F1][N4-R2].
- **Surface engineering strategies**: roughness and texture control, chemical modification, and hierarchical micro–nanostructuring [N1-F1][N2-R4].
- **Performance enhancement strategies**: self-healing, stimuli-responsive features, durable nanostructures, and multifunctional design [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R2].
- **Steel-specific considerations**: cleaning, conditioning, interfacial adhesion, and compatibility with steel chemistry [N1-F1][N4-R2][N6-F3].

Overall, the field is moving toward **multifunctional, durable, and environmentally responsive coatings** that can simultaneously suppress biofouling, protect against corrosion, and maintain long-term stability on steel surfaces [N1-F1][N3-R1][N5-R3][N6-F3]. The most successful coatings combine **low-surface-energy chemistry**, **surface roughness**, **functional anti-biofouling components**, and **steel-compatible preparation** into a single integrated design.

Fabrication techniques and surface engineering methods

Major coating fabrication methods and their advantages/disadvantages

The evidence points to a broad family of superhydrophobic coating fabrication strategies, with a clear distinction between top-down and bottom-up approaches. One review explicitly notes that fabrication methods include top-down methods such as laser ablation and etching, as well as bottom-up methods like sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R3]. A second source adds that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by creating the required surface roughness on a low-surface-energy material [N2-R4]. This suggests that the most common methods are either structuring the surface directly (top-down) or building up the coating layer by layer from molecular or particulate components (bottom-up).

The advantages of these methods vary by approach. Etching and template-based methods are attractive because they can produce well-controlled surface roughness and nanostructures, as shown in the one-step etching fabrication of a CuO/Cu2O/CuCl composite surface [N2-R2]. Similarly, sol–gel and templating can offer fine control over morphology [N2-R3]. However, these methods can also be more complex or require specialized equipment. The same source notes that fabrication techniques often still suffer from complexity, special conditions, or expensive equipment, which limits practical application [N2-F2]. For example, the one-step spray-coating method described in the PDMS/silica nanocomposite study is presented as a simpler, environmentally friendly alternative, but it still requires careful control of composition and spraying parameters to avoid excessive thickness or reduced transparency [N1-F1].

Surface roughness and texture engineering strategies

A central strategy for superhydrophobicity is surface roughness combined with low-surface-energy materials. The PDMS/silica study explicitly states that superhydrophobic surfaces are generally created by a micro–nanostructured rough surface and low-surface-energy material modification [N1-F1]. The same source describes a one-step spray-coating method that blends hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles with PDMS to form a hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader review, which emphasizes surface roughness as a key factor in superhydrophobic design [N2-R4].

The evidence also highlights texture engineering through the choice of particles and morphology. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study shows that mixing hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles in a certain ratio can produce a hierarchical structure that improves superhydrophobicity [N1-F1]. A separate review notes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by roughness engineering, with the roughness of the surface affecting transparency because light scattering increases with roughness [N1-F1]. This indicates that texture engineering is not only about creating roughness, but also about balancing roughness with optical and mechanical performance.

Chemical modification and functionalization approaches

Chemical modification is a recurring theme. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS as both a low-surface-energy modifier and an adhesive, and it also incorporates silica nanoparticles through a sol-gel-like route [N1-F1]. The same source notes that PDMS can be combined with SiO2 nanoparticles to form a rough structure, which is essential for superhydrophobicity [N1-R1]. Another search result explicitly states that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity or superoleophobicity [N1-R4], which reinforces that functionalization often involves adding low-surface-energy polymers or fluorinated components.

The evidence also supports the use of other functional components. The one-step etching fabrication example uses chemical etching and modification to create a superhydrophobic surface [N2-R2]. The broader fabrication review mentions vapor deposition, etching modification, sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R5], showing that chemical modification can be part of the fabrication process itself. In the steel-specific anti-corrosion context, a stearic acid–yttrium (SA–Y) superhydrophobic coating is prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2], which illustrates how chemical modification can be integrated into coating formation.

Steel-specific surface preparation and how it affects coating performance

Steel surface preparation matters because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The steel-specific anti-corrosion review notes that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This implies that surface preparation must support good adhesion and prevent corrosion pathways.

The evidence also shows that surface preparation can involve cleaning and conditioning. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study describes substrate cleaning with deionized water and alcohol before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared on low manganese steel by electrodeposition, which indicates that steel chemistry and surface state can influence coating formation [N4-R2]. The corrosion protection review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4], which means that even minor surface contamination or poor conditioning can degrade performance.

Overall, steel-specific preparation is important because it affects adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. The evidence suggests that successful coating performance depends on a combination of proper surface cleaning, conditioning, and chemical modification, rather than coating formulation alone [N4-R2][N1-F1][N6-F3].

This suggests that coatings may be designed to both repel microorganisms and kill them, especially in high-shear environments where fouling-release becomes important [N3-R5]. Fabrication techniques and surface engineering methods

Major coating fabrication methods and their advantages/disadvantages

The evidence points to a broad family of superhydrophobic coating fabrication strategies, with a clear distinction between top-down and bottom-up approaches. One review explicitly notes that fabrication methods include top-down methods such as laser ablation and etching, as well as bottom-up methods like sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R3]. A second source adds that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by creating the required surface roughness on a low-surface-energy material [N2-R4]. This suggests that the most common methods are either structuring the surface directly (top-down) or building up the coating layer by layer from molecular or particulate components (bottom-up).

The advantages of these methods vary by approach. Etching and template-based methods are attractive because they can produce well-controlled surface roughness and nanostructures, as shown in the one-step etching fabrication of a CuO/Cu2O/CuCl composite surface [N2-R2]. Similarly, sol–gel and templating can offer fine control over morphology [N2-R3]. However, these methods can also be more complex or require specialized equipment. The same source notes that fabrication techniques often still suffer from complexity, special conditions, or expensive equipment, which limits practical application [N2-F2]. For example, the one-step spray-coating method described in the PDMS/silica nanocomposite study is presented as a simpler, environmentally friendly alternative, but it still requires careful control of composition and spraying parameters to avoid excessive thickness or reduced transparency [N1-F1].

Surface roughness and texture engineering strategies

A central strategy for superhydrophobicity is surface roughness combined with low-surface-energy materials. The PDMS/silica study explicitly states that superhydrophobic surfaces are generally created by a micro–nanostructured rough surface and low-surface-energy material modification [N1-F1]. The same source describes a one-step spray-coating method that blends hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles with PDMS to form a hierarchical micro–nanostructured surface [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader review, which emphasizes surface roughness as a key factor in superhydrophobic design [N2-R4].

The evidence also highlights texture engineering through the choice of particles and morphology. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study shows that mixing hydrophilic and hydrophobic silica nanoparticles in a certain ratio can produce a hierarchical structure that improves superhydrophobicity [N1-F1]. A separate review notes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be fabricated by roughness engineering, with the roughness of the surface affecting transparency because light scattering increases with roughness [N1-F1]. This indicates that texture engineering is not only about creating roughness, but also about balancing roughness with optical and mechanical performance.

Chemical modification and functionalization approaches

Chemical modification is a recurring theme. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS as both a low-surface-energy modifier and an adhesive, and it also incorporates silica nanoparticles through a sol-gel-like route [N1-F1]. The same source notes that PDMS can be combined with SiO2 nanoparticles to form a rough structure, which is essential for superhydrophobicity [N1-R1]. Another search result explicitly states that silicone- or fluoro-based polymers are the main polymeric materials used to achieve superhydrophobicity or superoleophobicity [N1-R4], which reinforces that functionalization often involves adding low-surface-energy polymers or fluorinated components.

The evidence also supports the use of other functional components. The one-step etching fabrication example uses chemical etching and modification to create a superhydrophobic surface [N2-R2]. The broader fabrication review mentions vapor deposition, etching modification, sol–gel, template, electrostatic spinning, and electrostatic methods [N2-R5], showing that chemical modification can be part of the fabrication process itself. In the steel-specific anti-corrosion context, a stearic acid–yttrium (SA–Y) superhydrophobic coating is prepared by electrodeposition on low manganese steel [N4-R2], which illustrates how chemical modification can be integrated into coating formation.

Steel-specific surface preparation and how it affects coating performance

Steel surface preparation matters because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The steel-specific anti-corrosion review notes that superhydrophobic coatings for metal protection isolate the metal from corrosive media through water repellency, inhibition of electrochemical reactions, and enhanced interfacial adhesion [N6-F3]. This implies that surface preparation must support good adhesion and prevent corrosion pathways.

The evidence also shows that surface preparation can involve cleaning and conditioning. The PDMS/silica nanocomposite study describes substrate cleaning with deionized water and alcohol before spray coating [N1-F1]. The SA–Y coating is prepared on low manganese steel by electrodeposition, which indicates that steel chemistry and surface state can influence coating formation [N4-R2]. The corrosion protection review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings can prevent water or other corrosion-causing materials from absorbing into the surface [N6-R4], which means that even minor surface contamination or poor conditioning can degrade performance.

Overall, steel-specific preparation is important because it affects adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. The evidence suggests that successful coating performance depends on a combination of proper surface cleaning, conditioning, and chemical modification, rather than coating formulation alone [N4-R2][N1-F1][N6-F3].

Mechanisms and performance enhancement strategies

How the coating suppresses biofouling and prevents microbial adhesion

The evidence points to several mechanisms by which coatings suppress biofouling. One mechanism is surface chemistry repulsion, including hydration layer formation, surface charge repulsion, hydrophobic foul-release, and other biofouling-inhibiting effects [N3-R4]. Another search result describes zwitterionic hydrogel nanolayers that resist biofouling through the foulant repulsion of hydration shells and bactericidal effects [N3-R2]. A related study on photografted zwitterionic materials notes that antifouling effects are achievable across a broad range of cross-link densities, while maintaining mechanical functionality [N3-R1]. This indicates that biofouling suppression is not limited to one pathway but can combine multiple mechanisms.

The anti-biofouling strategy can also involve integrated antifouling and antimicrobial approaches. One source states that integrated antifouling and antimicrobial approaches are developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N3-R5]. This suggests that coatings may be designed to both repel microorganisms and kill them, especially in high-shear environments where fouling-release becomes important [N3-R5]. The evidence therefore supports a layered strategy: repelling microbes through surface chemistry, preventing adhesion through hydration or charge effects, and optionally killing organisms through antimicrobial components.

Strategies to improve durability and resistance to environmental stress

Durability is addressed through both material selection and fabrication methods. The PDMS/silica study shows that a one-step spray-coating method can produce coatings that remain superhydrophobic even after 250 tape peel cycles, UV exposure, and immersion in strong acid/base solutions for 72 h [N1-F1]. This is a clear durability demonstration. Another review emphasizes that superhydrophobic surfaces can be durable if transparency and roughness are balanced to reduce light scattering [N1-F1], which suggests that environmental stress is not only mechanical but also optical and chemical.

A separate review on recent advances in superhydrophobic materials development highlights durable nanostructures and intrinsic durability as key considerations [N5-R2]. This implies that durability is achieved through material architecture rather than surface chemistry alone. The same review also notes that the integration of durable nanostructures improves performance [N5-R1], which aligns with the broader idea that mechanical robustness is essential for long-term use.

Hybrid or multifunctional design features and their benefits

Hybrid or multifunctional designs are a major theme. The evidence repeatedly refers to multifunctional systems. The PDMS/silica study uses PDMS and silica nanoparticles together to create a superhydrophobic coating with good self-cleaning ability [N1-F1]. The dual-coating method combines polydimethylsiloxane-fluorine and fluorinated silica to create superhydrophobic, bacteriostatic surfaces [N1-R2]. This indicates that multifunctionality is often achieved by combining different materials or functional groups.

Another example is the use of zwitterionic materials with photografting to maintain antifouling while preserving mechanical properties [N3-R1]. This is a hybrid design because it combines antifouling chemistry with mechanical functionality. The review on recent advances also emphasizes bio-inspired design and durable nanostructures, showing that multifunctionality is not only about anti-biofouling but also about long-term performance [N5-R2][N5-R1].

Self-healing or stimuli-responsive features and their role in long-term stability

Self-healing and stimuli-responsive features are important for long-term stability. The review on recent advances in self-healing chemistries and approaches covers intrinsic and extrinsic self-healing strategies [N5-R3]. A separate study on superhydrophobic coatings with photothermal self-healing shows excellent self-healing performance in response to chemical and microstructure damage, with rapid self-healing under 1 sun [N5-R4]. This demonstrates that stimuli-responsive systems can repair damage and maintain performance.

The evidence also supports broader stimuli-responsive strategies. A review on smart antibacterial antifouling strategies notes that a variety of smart strategies have been developed to prevent bacterial contamination of biological surfaces [N5-R5]. While this excerpt is not specific to superhydrophobic coatings, it reinforces the general trend toward responsive materials. Together, these sources show that self-healing and stimuli-responsive features extend stability by repairing damage and adapting to environmental changes [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Overall, the coating suppresses biofouling through surface chemistry repulsion, hydration, charge effects, and optionally antimicrobial action [N3-R4][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Durability is improved by combining low-surface-energy materials with robust fabrication methods and by balancing roughness with transparency [N1-F1][N5-R2]. Hybrid or multifunctional designs combine anti-biofouling with mechanical or chemical functionality [N1-R2][N3-R1]. Self-healing and stimuli-responsive features improve long-term stability by repairing damage and adapting to environmental stress [N5-R3][N5-R4].

Steel surface preparation steps and why they matter

Steel surface preparation is critical because the substrate must be chemically and physically compatible with the coating. The evidence shows that preparation often begins with cleaning. The PDMS/silica study describes substrate cleaning with deionized water and alcohol before spray coating [N1-F1]. The anti-corrosion review emphasizes that superhydrophobic coatings isolate the metal from corrosive media, suggesting that a clean, well-prepared surface is needed to prevent contamination from the outset [N6-F3].

Why surface preparation matters includes adhesion, interfacial compatibility, and corrosion resistance. A clean surface improves coating adhesion and reduces defects such as delamination or poor bonding [N1-F1][N4-R2]. It also affects how the coating interacts with the steel substrate: if the surface is contaminated or not properly conditioned, the coating may not spread evenly or may fail at the interface [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The evidence further indicates that preparation affects long-term performance, because poor surface conditioning can compromise the protective role of the coating [N6-F3].
